title: Housing security has payment, coverage, hazard, and backstop layers that do not yet form a move outcome
source_unit: Deliberately non-pooled comparison of Federal Reserve household survey, Treasury/FIO insurance-market data, FEMA hazard context, and California FAIR Plan stocks
geography: United States with California residual-market case

observations.period: 2024-2025; Federal Reserve household housing and insurance module

denominator.unit: weighted renter or homeowner adult population estimates; conditional affordability questions have separate frames

low_income_neighborhood_without_insuranc.unit: percent of homeowners in low/moderate-income neighborhoods

insured_low_income_struggle_premiums.unit: percent of insured homeowners with income below $50,000

observations.method: Federal Reserve 2024 and 2025 SHED housing estimates; rent arrears, insurance status, and conditional affordability are kept as separate cross-sectional endpoints.
observations.uncertainty: Separate annual samples do not track the same households; self-reports do not identify arrears duration, eviction, policy terms, hazard exposure, claims, repairs, mortgage status, or move/stay outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Renters and homeowners, conditioned by income and neighborhood income where reported.
observations.counterinterpretation: Arrears do not equal eviction, and no insurance can reflect self-insurance or preference as well as affordability; premium struggle does not prove inadequate coverage or insurer withdrawal.

observations.period: 2018-2022; Treasury FIO homeowners-insurance market by climate-risk ZIP group and FEMA context

denominator.unit: matched Treasury ZIP rows for FEMA context; national FIO analysis covers more than 246 million policies

highest_climate_risk_nonrenewal_differen.unit: percent above lowest-risk ZIP quintile, approximate

fema_low_vs_very_high_nonrenewal.unit: percent unweighted mean nonrenewal by FEMA rating

observations.method: Treasury FIO ZIP-code insurance data are grouped by expected annual building losses and joined to FEMA NRI county context through Census ZCTA relationships; policy-weighted and unweighted estimates remain distinct.
observations.uncertainty: The 2018-2022 window predates later market conditions; ZIP/county assignment, modeled hazard, insurer mix, property composition, regulation, rebuilding costs, and reporting coverage confound interpretation. The non-monotonic FEMA premium pattern is retained.
observations.subgroup: Climate-risk ZIP quintiles and FEMA Expected Annual Loss rating groups; market rows are not households.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher risk aligns with higher market premiums/nonrenewal in the broad comparison, but hazard bins do not establish causal pricing or household coverage loss; very-high FEMA rows do not have the highest mean premium in the derived screen.

denominator.unit: matched Treasury ZIP rows with usable ACS ZCTA context; unweighted row means

observations.method: Descriptive unweighted means of Treasury ZIP rows matched to ACS ZCTAs and grouped by median household income and owner-share context; ZIP and ZCTA are treated as an approximation.
observations.uncertainty: Place context is not the income, tenure, or insurance status of individual policyholders. Exposure, property type, value, insurer mix, hazard, and reporting selection remain uncontrolled.
observations.subgroup: Matched ZIP/ZCTA rows by ACS median household income and owner-share bands.
observations.counterinterpretation: The non-monotonic premium pattern and higher lower-income-place nonrenewal do not identify an individual affordability or displacement gradient; urban property mix and hazard may dominate.

observations.period: September 2021-September 2025 and June 2026; California FAIR Plan residual-market stock

denominator.unit: California FAIR Plan total policy/exposure stock across published lines; current headline scope differs from fiscal-year report

observations.method: California FAIR Plan fiscal-year county-report totals and later quarterly key-statistics headline; policy count, insured exposure, premium, and scope changes are kept separate.
observations.uncertainty: Residual-market growth is not a direct count of households denied voluntary insurance; line-of-business, fiscal timing, coverage limits, valuation, insurer mix, replacement, and reporting changes matter. The series does not observe repairs or moves.
observations.subgroup: California FAIR Plan residential, commercial, and business-owner lines in the fiscal series; later headline covers dwelling and commercial scope.
observations.counterinterpretation: A growing public backstop can reflect risk, prices, underwriting, policy design, or improved enrollment visibility; it does not alone prove private-market withdrawal, unaffordability, or displacement.

related_sources.claim: Federal Reserve supplies household rent-arrears, insurance-gap, and affordability endpoints.
Treasury FIO supplies national ZIP-level premium, nonrenewal, claim, and coverage context.
FEMA NRI join supplies modeled hazard context and non-monotonic counterexample.
California FAIR Plan supplies a later public-backstop stock and exposure series.

boundary: This is a non-pooled housing-payment/coverage/hazard/backstop bridge. It supports a staged picture of housing security but does not establish household-level affordability, coverage adequacy, insurer causation, repairs, lending, move/stay outcomes, public legitimacy, or political response. A compatible property/household-year panel with claims, assistance, repair, and mobility outcomes remains open.
